paragraphs.text: Around 40% of what people do each day is not the result of conscious decisions but of habits, according to research by the psychologist Wendy Wood. We brush our teeth, check our phones and take the same route to work largely without thinking. This is not a weakness. Habits free the mind to concentrate on new or difficult problems; a person who had to deliberate over every small action would be exhausted by lunchtime.

Habits form through repetition in a stable context. When an action is repeatedly performed in the same situation and is followed by a reward, the brain gradually links the situation directly to the action. Eventually, the situation alone is enough to trigger the behaviour. The journalist Charles Duhigg popularised this process as a 'habit loop' consisting of a cue, a routine and a reward. In my view, his model is useful as a simple guide, although it makes habit formation sound more mechanical than it really is.

How long does it take to form a new habit? A widely repeated claim is that it takes 21 days. This figure appears to come from a 1960 book by a plastic surgeon, Maxwell Maltz, who observed that patients took about three weeks to get used to a change in their appearance; he was not studying habits at all. A 2009 study by Phillippa Lally at University College London followed volunteers trying to adopt simple behaviours, such as drinking water after breakfast. On average, it took 66 days for the behaviour to become automatic, but the range was enormous, from 18 to 254 days.

Lally's study also produced an encouraging finding: missing a single day did not seriously affect the process. This matters because many people abandon a new routine after one failure, believing that they have ruined their progress. It is far more important, I would argue, to return to the routine quickly than to maintain a perfect record.

Breaking bad habits is harder than forming good ones, because the link between cue and response remains in the brain even when we no longer act on it. Willpower alone is an unreliable solution. Wood's research suggests that successful people do not have more self-control than others; instead, they arrange their environment to avoid temptation. Someone who wants to eat less sugar, for example, is better off not keeping sweets at home than trying to resist them every evening. Changes of environment, such as moving house or starting a new job, also offer a valuable opportunity, since old cues disappear.
